2000 CanLII 21339 (CA IRB)
1 AA0-00163/168 
 ORAL DECISION AND REASONS
 These are the reasons for the decision in the claim of XXXXXXX, file number AA0-00163 and XXXXXXXXX , file number AA0-00168, to be Conve ntion refugees. The reasons have been edited for grammar, syntax, spelling and punctuation, and may include references to applicable case law. BY PRESIDING MEMBER
 These are the reasons for decision in the claim to be a refugee of XXXXXXXX, file number AAO-00163 and of XXXXXXXXXX, f ile number AAO-00168. The principal claimant XXXXXXXX is the designated representative of the minor claimant XXXXXXXX because she was born in 1989, and she is a minor. The claimant is making a claim basically on gender grounds. She says she was a victim of domestic violence in the state of Michigan, and that she left her husband a few times,but he had found her in shelters, and in the residence of the principal claimant's siblings and begged her to go back. She went back to him several times. However, in XXXXXX of 1999, she left for Tennessee. He found her there also because the claimant had written to the school of the daughter and had given her address. This is how the husband found out where she was. He went to Tennessee and started making telephone calls to her. He had made telephone calls to her even before going to Tennessee, and in addition, he kept visiting her to see his daughter On these occasions he also begged of her to go to back to him. He parked his van in the parking lot of the hospital in an area where he could see when she was going from the road, anywhere, and he often followed her, but he kept a distance because of the restraining order. The claimant said that she had police protection. The police had said very clearly to give them a call when 
2000 CanLII 21339 (CA IRB)
2 AA0-00163/168 
 she needed them. When she called them they were there. But she says the police cannot protect her 24 hours a day, seven days a week. The claimant came to Canada to attend a wedding, and the friends who brought her to Canada for the wedding took her back to Tennessee, but brought her back because she liked it here and felt safer. The claimant is of the opinion that her husband would be able to find her anywhere in the United States. We asked her how would he find her if she were to move to California or Florida, Arizona, Oregon, Washington D.C., New York, Vermont, etc. She stated that she thought that he would be able to find out. The Panel asked her, "How would he be able to find out when he is only a dishwasher and a cook and a man of poor means?" She said that he is not a man of poor means, that he is a drug addict, alcoholic and a mental patient, but because of his drug dealings he has money and that he can find out where she is. Then the Panel asked her that "When he did know where you were and when he was close to you, at least physically, he made no effort to harm you beyond requesting you or asking you or threatening you to go back, but he did so verbally." She said this is true. He did not, in Tennessee, when she had left him and was living with friends try to physically harm her, although he had done so earlier in their marriage, but that because of his mental situation and his alcoholism she is afraid and she doesn't know whether he'd try to harm her. He had made threats in the past to kill her, and he also shot at her picture. So she feels, therefore, afraid. The case law is that there is a presumption of state protection, and it's only if the state is unwilling or unable to protect the claimant that the claimant could then seek international protection. The documentary evidence is that there is protection available in the U.S. The judiciary is free. The police is available to citizens to protect them 
2000 CanLII 21339 (CA IRB)
3 AA0-00163/168 
 from violence, from husbands or from others, although, as the claimant said, such protection is not available 24 hours a day, and this is what case law also says, that nobody can be guaranteed 100 per cent protection. However, the protection should be available and it is available to the claimant in the United States. It's also not clear to the Panel how would the husband able to find her if the claimant, who is educated, who has a high school diploma and who also upgraded her high school education and was working, and who has family. Now, it's not clear how the claimant would be in danger if she were to go to any of the other states. The United States is a huge country of 250 million people. The claimant could easily live in any state other than Michigan or Tennessee even. The only time that he was able to find out was when she sent the school information about her address, and secondly, when she had already gone to her siblings nearby. So he went to the sibling's house and found her. If she were to go to California or Oregon or Florida or New Mexico, any state in this the United States, it is not clear to the Panel that the man would have the means to find out. And even if he had the means to find out where she is, she had protection available through the American authorities, and in fact, this protection was offered to her in the past. So for these reasons we find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee because she has an IFA as well as state protection in her own country. She says that she feels safer in Canada because her husband will not be allowed to enter Canada because of some charge or some disqualification, but she also testified that she was able to come to Canada simply because the border authorities did not even check her papers. So it is reasonable to infer that if he wanted to come to Canada, he could do so, perhaps not by air, but driving through with friends and others. So this way, if he can find her in the United States, he could try to look for her in Canada. The Panel does not feel that it's reasonable to infer that he will be able to find her in Canada or the United States, and she also has internal flight alternative in the U.S. 
2000 CanLII 21339 (CA IRB)
4 AA0-00163/168 
 So we do not find that the pr incipal claimant, XXXXXXXXXX, is a Convention refugee or that she meets the requirements of the Immigration Act because she has protection available as well as internal flight alternative in her own country. As far as the minor claimant is concerned, she has said that what she fears is that if she goes back, her dad will find the two of them and he might hit her mother, as he had sometimes done in the past. But she says that she has no fear from her father herself, that he was nice to her when they were together in Tennessee as well as in Michigan. That's what the documentary evidence also says. The principal claimant said that when they were together, the father made the daughter sit on his lap, and as a victim of child rape, she is afraid for her daughter. But this speculation. In any case, if the daughter were to go back with her mother, it is reasonable to infer that the father will not be able to find them out, that they will be able to live in the United States. And if the principal claimant feels that the daughter is in some danger, she can get a restraining order from the courts. The judiciary in the United States is independent and is available and accessible to the average citizens. So for all these reasons I find that neither the principal claimant, nor the minor claimant meet the requirements of the Immigration Act and that they are not Convention refugees. I would request my colleague to offer her views. BY SECOND MEMBER
 - I concur, and I have nothing to add. Thank you.

 - Thank you very much. That concludes the hearing. This concludes the hearing in your case. Good luck. " A z h a r A l i K h a n " A z h a r A l i K h a n Concured in by: "XXXXXXXXXX" N y c o l e R o y Dated at Ottawa this 7th day of December, 2000.
